title: Falcons: The Fastest Hunters
summary: How falcons use sharp eyes, fast dives, and strong talons to hunt, and why falconry is an important tradition in Saudi Arabia.
poll: Falcons are the most amazing birds in the world.

versions.title: Falcons Are Fast
versions.text:
Look up at the sky. Do you see that bird? It is a falcon. It is a fast bird. It hunts.

A falcon has sharp eyes. It can see a small bird far off. It flies up high. Then it folds its wings. It drops down in a dive. It goes as fast as a jet!

The peregrine falcon is the fastest of all. In a dive, it can go more than 300 km each hour. No car on a road is that fast.

The bird it hunts is its prey. A falcon grabs its prey in the air. It holds it with its talons. Talons are sharp claws. Its beak has a hook. It is strong.

The mom is big. The dad is not as big.

In Saudi Arabia, men and boys train falcons. This is old. They use a thick glove. The bird sits on it. They put a hood on its head. The hood keeps the bird calm. Each year, there is a big falcon show.

versions.text:

A falcon has amazing eyes. It can spot a small bird from very far away. First, the falcon climbs high into the air. Then it tucks its wings close to its body. It drops toward the ground in a steep dive. It moves as fast as a jet plane!

versions.title: Falcons: The Fastest Hunters
versions.text:
High above the desert, a bird glides in slow circles. Suddenly it folds its wings and plunges toward the ground. This bird is a falcon, one of the most skillful hunters in the sky.

A falcon is a predator, which means it hunts other animals for food. Its eyesight is much sharper than a person's. From high in the air, it can notice a small bird moving far below. When it is ready, the falcon tucks its wings against its body and drops in a steep dive called a stoop.

The peregrine falcon is the fastest animal on Earth. During a stoop, it can reach more than 300 kilometers per hour. That is faster than a racing car on a straight track.

Most falcons catch other birds in the air. A falcon strikes its prey with its talons, the sharp, curved claws on its feet. Its strong beak has a hook and a small notch that helps it hold its food.

Female falcons are larger than males, often by about one third.

Training falcons to hunt is called falconry. In Saudi Arabia, falconry is an old tradition that families have passed down for many generations. A falconer wears a thick leather glove for the bird to perch on. A small hood covers the bird's eyes and keeps it calm. Each year, falconers gather at a large festival to celebrate their birds.

versions.title: Falcons: Masters of Speed
versions.text:
High above the desert, a bird glides in slow, wide circles, carefully scanning the ground beneath it. Without warning, it folds its wings and plunges toward the earth like a falling arrow. This remarkable creature is a falcon, one of the most accomplished and efficient predators in the sky.

A falcon's eyesight is several times sharper than a human's, which enables it to detect a small bird moving far below. When the opportunity arrives, the falcon pulls its wings tightly against its body, creating a streamlined shape that slices through the air with little resistance, and descends in a steep dive known as a stoop.

The peregrine falcon is generally considered the fastest animal on Earth, since its velocity during a stoop can exceed 300 kilometers per hour. Small bony cones, called tubercles, inside its nostrils appear to moderate the rushing air so that the bird can keep breathing. A thin third eyelid also sweeps across each eye, protecting it from wind and dust.

Most falcons capture other birds in midair. A falcon strikes its prey with its talons, the sharp, curved claws on its feet, and its powerful beak has a hook and a small notch that help it grip and finish its catch. Females are usually about one third larger than males, which allows them to capture heavier prey.

During the twentieth century, peregrine numbers fell sharply because a pesticide called DDT made their eggshells so thin that they cracked. After many countries banned the chemical, the birds gradually recovered.

The practice of training falcons to hunt is called falconry, and in Saudi Arabia it is an ancient tradition that families have passed down through many generations. A falconer wears a thick leather glove so that the bird can perch safely, while a small leather hood covers its eyes and keeps it calm. In 2010, falconry was added to a UNESCO list of the world's cultural heritage, and Saudi Arabia was among the countries that requested it. Each year, falconers travel to a major festival in Saudi Arabia to celebrate their birds.

versions.title: Falcons: Masters of Speed
versions.text:
High above the desert, a solitary bird glides in slow, sweeping circles, methodically surveying the terrain beneath it. Without warning, it folds its wings and plunges toward the earth like a descending arrow. This remarkable creature is a falcon, one of the most accomplished and efficient predators in the natural world, and its hunting technique has fascinated observers for thousands of years.

A falcon's eyesight is several times sharper than a human's, which enables it to identify a small bird moving across the landscape far below. When the opportunity materializes, the falcon draws its wings tightly against its body, creating a streamlined profile that penetrates the atmosphere with minimal resistance, and descends in a precipitous dive known as a stoop.

The peregrine falcon is generally considered the fastest animal on Earth, because its velocity during a stoop can exceed 300 kilometers per hour. Small bony cones, called tubercles, positioned inside its nostrils apparently moderate the rushing air so that the bird can continue breathing comfortably at such extraordinary speeds. Additionally, a transparent third eyelid periodically sweeps across each eye, protecting it from turbulent wind and airborne debris.

Most falcons capture other birds in midair. A falcon strikes its prey with its talons, the sharp, curved claws on its feet, and its powerful beak possesses a hook and a small notch that help it secure and dispatch its catch. Females are typically about one third larger than males, which enables them to overpower considerably heavier prey.

During the twentieth century, peregrine populations declined dramatically because a pesticide called DDT accumulated in their bodies and rendered their eggshells so fragile that they fractured during incubation. After numerous countries prohibited the chemical, the birds gradually recovered, demonstrating convincingly that deliberate environmental protection can reverse serious ecological damage.

The practice of training falcons to hunt is called falconry, and in Saudi Arabia it represents an ancient tradition that families have transmitted through many generations. A falconer wears a thick leather glove so that the bird can perch securely, while a small leather hood covers its eyes and keeps it tranquil. In 2010, falconry was officially incorporated into a UNESCO list of the world's intangible cultural heritage, and Saudi Arabia was among the countries that requested this international recognition. Annually, falconers travel considerable distances to a prestigious festival in Saudi Arabia to celebrate their extraordinary birds.

HIGH.prompt: The article says that environmental protection can reverse serious damage. Explain how the story of the peregrine falcon supports this idea, and suggest one way people can protect birds today.
checklist: I explained how the peregrine's story supports the idea.
I used specific evidence from the article.
I suggested one realistic way to protect birds today.
HIGH.modelAnswer: The peregrine falcon's story shows that environmental protection can reverse serious damage, because the pesticide DDT once built up in their bodies and made their eggshells so thin that they cracked during incubation, causing populations to decline dramatically. After many countries banned DDT, the falcons gradually recovered, proving that a harmful human action can be undone once people change their behavior. To protect birds today, people could avoid using harmful chemical pesticides near natural habitats, since this same kind of pollution is what nearly destroyed the peregrine falcon in the past.
